blogs.title: Strict Adherence Meets Automated Cancellation: How Far Can Courts Modernize Statutory Procedures Without Rewriting Them?
blogs.description: This post examines the tension at the heart of Williams v. GoAuto between Louisiana's strict adherence doctrine for insurance-premium finance cancellations and the Fifth Circuit's willingness to accept fully automated, computer-driven cancellation processes. The court acknowledged that strict adherence serves critical functions—fixing the exact time of cancellation and providing a minimum cure period—yet held that a process involving no human review before cancellation satisfies the statute. The post will analyze whether the court's reasoning is consistent with the doctrine's protective purposes, or whether it effectively rewrites the statute by interpreting 'certifying' and 'receipt' to accommodate modern automation, and what this means for the future of consumer-protective statutory formalities in an era of algorithmic processing.

blogs.title: What Does It Mean to 'Certify'? The Fifth Circuit's Textualist Reading of Louisiana's Cancellation Statute
blogs.description: This post focuses on the court's textualist interpretation of the word 'certifying' in Louisiana Revised Statute § 9:3550(G)(3)(a), concluding that no signature is required before a policy can be cancelled. The post will analyze the court's reasoning that because the statute identifies the 'insurance premium finance company'—rather than a named individual—as the entity that certifies, a corporate certification without a human signature suffices. It will explore the implications of this holding for the broader law of certifications, affirmations, and attestations: if a corporation can 'certify' through automated electronic transmission without any identified human actor, what becomes of the evidentiary and accountability functions that signatures traditionally serve? The post will also discuss how the court navigated the near-total absence of Louisiana precedent on this question.

blogs.title: 'Receipt' in the Age of APIs: Statutory Interpretation When Computers Talk to Computers
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's interpretation of 'receipt' under Louisiana's insurance-premium finance statute, holding that GoAuto's computer system effecting cancellation upon receiving an automated electronic transmission from APAC's system satisfies the statutory requirement that the insurer 'receive' the cancellation request. The post will explore the broader implications of this holding for federal courts interpreting state statutes drafted in pre-digital eras: when a statute says an entity must 'receive' something, and the entity's computer receives it automatically without any human awareness, has 'receipt' occurred? The post will discuss the court's reliance on Black's Law Dictionary definitions of 'receipt' and 'receive,' the conceptual gap between physical-possession definitions and automated electronic processing, and how courts should approach similar statutory terms that predate modern computing.

blogs.title: The Fifth Circuit's Reluctance to Certify Novel State-Law Questions: A Pattern or a Problem?
blogs.description: This post examines the Fifth Circuit's denial of the plaintiffs' request to certify the novel questions of Louisiana statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court. The court invoked its self-described reluctance to 'go to that well too often' and held that the mere absence of a state supreme court definition is insufficient to warrant certification. The post will analyze this decision in the context of Erie principles and the certification process more broadly: when a federal appellate court confronts genuinely unsettled questions of state law with significant implications for an entire state's insurance industry, what threshold should trigger certification? The post will discuss whether the Fifth Circuit's restrictive approach to certification risks making federal courts de facto arbiters of state statutory meaning, and how this case fits into broader patterns of the Fifth Circuit's certification jurisprudence.
